# Why does my 2005 Mitsubishi Pajero use excessive amounts of fuel?

A 30-litre-per-100km consumption rate on a 2005 Mitsubishi Pajero is a significant deviation from factory specifications, especially when intake and exhaust systems have been verified as functional. When standard mechanical checks like spark plugs, air filters, and throttle bodies yield no results, the problem often shifts from simple component failure to data integrity or control logic issues. The engine control unit (ECU) relies on specific inputs to determine fuel delivery; if those inputs are corrupted or misinterpreted, the system will inject more fuel than necessary to maintain target combustion ratios.

One of the most common culprits in vehicles of this era is the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor calibration drift. Over time, the internal heater element or the sensing wire can degrade, causing the sensor to report higher airflow values than reality. If the ECU believes more air is entering the intake than is actually present, it enriches the fuel mixture to compensate, resulting in high consumption. While replacing the sensor is a standard repair, the root cause might be electrical noise or grounding issues affecting the signal line. Before condemning the hardware, inspect the wiring harness for chafing against the chassis and ensure the ground strap near the ECU is clean and tight.

Another frequent issue involves the oxygen sensors located in the exhaust stream. The upstream sensor (pre-catalyst) provides real-time feedback to the ECU for closed-loop fuel control. If this sensor fails or gets contaminated by oil blow-by, it may send a lean signal when the mixture is actually rich. The ECU interprets this as insufficient fuel and injects even more, creating a positive feedback loop of excessive consumption. Since you have ruled out exhaust problems broadly, focus specifically on the sensor's electrical output rather than physical blockage. A multimeter or oscilloscope can reveal if the sensor is stuck in a lean state despite a rich mixture.

Fuel pressure regulation is also a critical variable often overlooked. The fuel pump relay and the fuel pressure regulator must maintain precise line pressure. If the regulator fails internally, allowing pressure to drop too low, the ECU compensates by widening the injector pulse width to deliver the required mass of fuel. This results in poor atomization and inefficient combustion, driving up consumption. Check the return line for restrictions and verify that the fuel pressure holds steady under load without dipping excessively.

Transmission shifting patterns can also impact overall efficiency. If the torque converter clutch does not lock up properly or if the transmission is stuck in a higher gear than appropriate for road speed, engine RPMs will remain elevated, increasing fuel use. Verify shift points by monitoring RPM at specific speeds; inconsistent delays in upshifts often point to low fluid levels or failing solenoids within the TCU.

Finally, consider the possibility of a vacuum leak that is not immediately visible. A small leak can introduce unmetered air after the MAF sensor, confusing the ECU's air-fuel ratio calculation. Listen for hissing sounds near the intake manifold gasket and inspect all vacuum hoses for cracks. Even minor leaks can skew the lambda sensor readings significantly enough to cause measurable fuel waste. Addressing these electrical and pressure-related variables usually resolves consumption issues that mechanical inspections alone cannot fix.
